questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I am studying Japanese Studies. And I chose Ochanomizu Uni. for several reasons, including the central location in Tokyo, inexpensive on-campus housing with a private room and its own bathroom and kitchenette, as well as the university's great focus on women's progress in academia and business.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
1. I received a lot of information about orientation and arrival by mail in the weeks and days prior to my departure from DK. There were also regular Zoom meetings with the Home Room teacher and the international students (both one-on-one and altogether).
2. If I had questions, I would either ask at these meetings or contact the International Office at Ochanomizu Uni. 
3. However, the only downside to the process was that Ochanomizu Uni. was quite late in announcing the move-in date. They encouraged the international students to arrive at the end of September to be sure, and so we only had a very short time to move-in before the semester started.
 (We could move-in on September 30, there was campus-orientation on September 31, and the semester began on October 1).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
1. I had received many documents from Ochanomizu Uni., which should prepare me for the arrival and the first days on campus. Including instructions on how to get from the airport to campus.
2. There are a few mandatory orientation meetings on the day of arrival and the following days (about the housing, campus and the surrounding area). 
3. There are regular meetings once a week with all international students in a class called "Home Room". The Home Room teacher and the international students discuss things such as important deadlines, guidelines, rules, events and more.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
The on-campus housing is called Otowakan. It was great and inexpensive, totally recommended.
The only option is a private room which consists of a balcony, toilet, shower and kitchenette.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
There is a cafeteria on campus, right outside Otowakan. 
The students, residents at Otowakan, and some of the professors, often eat lunch and dinner there. 
There is a communal kitchen in Otowakan, which can be booked ahead of time if someone wishes to access other cooking facilities than those available in the private kitchenette.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
I recommend applying for the on-campus housing. It's convenient, the dormitory/reception staff is super helpful and nice, and you have a higher chance of socializing with other students (both international and Japanese) on a daily basis. 
Otowakan houses both Japanese and international students, but there is a much bigger ratio of Japanese students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration process is a bit complicated. You have to create a trial/ first version course registration sheet to submit to your home room teacher. Afterwards, you will discuss this sheet and you might have to make changes to accommodate both Ochanomizu Uni., UCPH and yourself. Then you will have a chance to try courses in the first week of the semester, and make new changes to your sheet. 
You need to get your registration sheet confirmed and stamped by your academic supervisor before it's valid for a final course registration submission. Lastly, you have a short period in which you still have the option of dropping some courses, but you can't add anymore courses. 
So, the process is both online and on printed paper, and multiple people have to approve of the courses.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
1. There was information in the many documents received by mail. 
2. There were also multiple meetings about the process in the "Home Room"- class. 
3. The International Office on campus at Ochanomizu Uni. 
4. 2nd semester international students who knew of the process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Some courses were suddenly cancelled at the beginning of the semester, which is something that can happen, so I had to change my priorities. 
However, I was a 100% successful in the end.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't feel discouraged if you find anything challenging or difficult to understand - it's better to ask and get clarity as the registration process is very different to how it is at UCPH.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Some students who had been at Ochanomizu University for 2 semesters said that the Japanese courses in the Spring semester seemed more difficult than the ones in the Autumn/Fall semester. 
You take an online Japanese language comprehension test before your exchange, and the home room teacher will discuss the results with you and guide you on the level of the courses. 
However, you have a chance to try out different levels during the first week of the semester, before you have to make the final course registration. 
There are few courses in English, but they are interesting and the level is easy.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
UCPH has a ton of reading and preparation for each class (non-Japanese language class), whereas Ochanomizu University doesn't. It's more about participating in the class discussions following the professor's lecture - as there is a ton of group work and a lot of presentations. 

The teaching style of the Japanese language classes is somewhat more or less the same, but with more assignments, oral presentations and practically no use of English in class or learning documents. Sometimes there are tests more often throughout the semester, while some classes have a test each week.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
23A2415 Technology and Gender
23N0093 Facilitation 
23G0202 Seminar: Japanese Culture IB 
23B2045 Globalization and Labor I 
23B8510 Cultural Transformations I 
23B2026 Cultural and Human Relations I 

I also had Special Japanese Classes (Japanese language classes) besides the above mentioned courses. 
(Home Room is a mandatory class for international students, but not something to obtain credits from).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I'm not sure which courses I would recommend, but: 
1. "文化変動論"/ "Cultural Transformations" was an informative and easily comprehensive course about gender, migration and cultural transformation through time. We watched about 2-3 movies, which was a great way to further discussion and understanding. 
2. "テクノロジーとジェンダー"/ "Technology & Gender" had multiple class excursions to museums, although the professor could be difficult to understand at times. 
3. "Seminar: Japanese Culture IB" was a culture course with the nicest professor. She was very passionate about cultural exchange and her classes were interesting and down to earth - you also learned a lot about the cultures of your classmates.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Nothing I can think of.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
1. Eating out was less expensive. 
2. If you live on campus, you don't have to pay for daily use of public transportation, which is a big plus. I put 70 DKK as the cost of local transportation because I used it often to go explore in my spare time. 
3. Rent and gas are charged/billed and paid for seperatly - gas was less expensive than I expected. 
4. Well, most items were less expensive than I expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
1. There were multiple mandatory cultural exchange events with the participation of all international students and some Japanese students arranged by the university. 
2. There were various university clubs such as a tea ceremony club (with a real tea house on campus for that purpose).
3. Ochanomizu University School Festival.
4. There were multiple opportunities to participate in cultural and social activities through courses and events presented in mails from the university. These were free of charge and were only available for a limited number of participants, so you had to be quick to respond. 
Fx. ikebana class, kimono class, cooking class, kaligraphy class etc. 
5. There was a kind of fitness/yoga room available for booking in the dormitory. (With mirrors, not with fitness gear). It seemed like there might have been a regular dance/fitness club that booked the room sometime during the week. 
6. There was a Japanese café and an English café, established by the international students for language exchange once a week.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Well, all of the above. I didn't get to participate in the ikebana class because of my schedule, but the ones who did really enjoyed it. It's something you don't normally experience, and it's a dying activity in schools in Japan. 
These small cultural courses were casual and non-academic, with mostly Japanese instructors and international students. They weren't Japanese language classes or something to obtain credits from, so you can let loose, have fun and experience something new.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
1. Locally, definitely explore the area outside campus - just take a walk in the surrounding neighbourhood. It's quite interestingly something that many forget to do, because you live there for a longer amount of time and establish a routine. 
2. Locally, visit some of the nearby parks, gardens, temples and museums - you can reach many on foot. 
3. Walk from campus to nearby places like Ikebukuro or Shin-ōtsuka (lots and lots to do - fx. Sunshine City Mall in Ikebukuro). 
4. Visit Ochanomizu Station - you can take the metro. 
5. Attend festivals or markets depending on the time of your exchange and the season.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. The environment on campus as well as in the dormitory was welcoming. And the local culture in Bunkyō-ku, Tokyo, where Ochanomizu University is located, is quite down to earth. There are parks, temples and other cultural sights nearby - and the area is bustling with life at all times, especially at rush hour and on the weekends. The campus is very close to a metro station with a quick connection to the rest of central Tokyo.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: You can try to contact and befriend your assigned tutor, who will be a Japanese student. Otherwise, there are multiple university clubs (such as a tea ceremony club).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I sometimes found the indirect, read between the lines/not spoken, communication challenging. 
If possible, it might prove easier to receive a clearer answer by writing an email. For example, in regards to a professor or alike.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
Funnily enough, I really appreciated the queue culture. As well as the various opportunities to entertain yourself in different ways - you always experience something new. 
And how nature is such a big part of the culture.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Please feel free to contact and communicate with Ochanomizu University - both online and in person. They are super welcoming, quick to reply and wish you the best possible exchange experience.   
(It is better to ask once too much than once too little.)
2. There are some social and cultural events that are mandatory to participate in, but there are also other events with voluntary participation arranged by the university and the university clubs. These are chances to meet other students in a more casual and fun setting - although it might seem daunting at first, please try it out. 
3. You will also be assigned a tutor, who is a Japanese student, to assist you throughout the semester. It's an interesting concept, where you can help each other with Japanese and English, and you can meet up and go on trips together.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
1. You will be introduced to a service called Give-and-Take, which is unique to Ochanomizu University.
It's a website where former students and dormitory residents give away stuff for the new students and residents to take/make a reservation for. It's free of charge, you just put the stuff back on the website before your own departure. Please make use of it, it's quite nice. 
2. It's useful to know of a nearby medical clinic with English speaking personnel in case you get sick and need help/assistance/guidance. There is a very small medical clinic on campus, but you always have to make a booking in advance. 
The booking system is a bit complicated, the times are few and far between, and there is a lot they can't help with - so if you need help quickly, please seek out another option.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
I was lucky to meet some amazing people from Japan and around the world during my exchange - all of which lived in the same dormitory on campus as I did (the on-campus dormitory houses both international and Japanese students). So, sharing the exchange experience with my new friends was the most rewarding part. 
However, having the possibility of actually living in Japan for 4-5 months and experiencing different social and cultural contexts firsthand, have also put my education, interests and future into perspective.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The greatest challenge was all of the official paperwork, which seemed endless at times. 
There is a lot of paperwork before going abroad, but it's another level in Japan. 
You have to fill out a lot of documents on the day of moving into the dormitory, as well as going to the local Civic Center multiple times for other documents - there are even times, when everyone seems confused. This is on repeat throughout the semester, even in the very last days before departure. 
But: it's easier if you find someone and do it together.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
I think my semester abroad in Tokyo, Japan - particularly at Ochanomizu University - has truly been an unforgettable and unparalleled experience. 
There can be difficult and challenging times, but you can find a way to approach and overcome these - remember to also enjoy your time and have fun exploring daily life in Japan.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
